posts.title: Building a CHIP-8 Emulator in C
posts.excerpt: Fourteen bytes set up both paddles in Pong. Follow them from a ROM file into CHIP-8 memory and through my C disassembler.
posts.content:
The first fourteen bytes of the Pong ROM in my CHIP-8 project describe both paddles. Four instructions give their positions, one picks a sprite, and two draw it. Those bytes make a good tour of the code because you can follow them from a file on disk to an address in the emulated machine, then read what each instruction asks the machine to do. My C implementation gets as far as loading the ROM and producing that listing. Pong ROM.

Giving the ROM an address

I represented the machine in one C structure. It has 4,096 bytes of memory, sixteen byte-sized registers, a program counter, an index register called I, and room for sixteen return addresses. The screen is a 64 by 32 array laid out in one dimension. Initialization clears the arrays and sets the program counter to hexadecimal 0x200. It also copies eighty bytes of font data into low memory at 0x50. There are five rows for each hexadecimal digit, so the glyph for A begins at 0x82. Machine layout and font.

The ROM file starts at byte zero on disk, but its instructions use addresses relative to the machine. My loader writes file byte zero at 0x200, file byte one at 0x201, and so on. That leaves 3,584 bytes for a program. The loader checks that length, copies the bytes, and writes the whole memory image to memory.dump. You can inspect both the built-in font and the program in a single file. ROM loading and memory dump.

Reading Pong's opening instructions

From the checkout, make builds the command-line tool. Run ./emu -d roms/Pong.rom to see the disassembly. Each line includes the machine address, the two instruction bytes, and a mnemonic. Here are the first seven instructions with their operands written out in words. Instruction decoder.

0200  6A 02   Load VA with 2
0202  6B 0C   Load VB with 12
0204  6C 3F   Load VC with 63
0206  6D 0C   Load VD with 12
0208  A2 EA   Set I to 0x2EA
020A  DA B6   Draw 6 rows at (VA, VB)
020C  DC D6   Draw 6 rows at (VC, VD)

The pieces have different meanings depending on the first four bits. In 6A 02, the 6 selects a load, A identifies the destination register, and the entire second byte is the value. In A2 EA, three digits combine into one address. In DA B6, A and B name two registers, and 6 gives the sprite height. My decoder uses a shift to select the instruction family, then masks or shifts the remaining bits according to that family's format. Address and sprite decoding.

You can check the paddle shape independently. Run ./emu -f roms/Pong.rom, then od -An -tx1 -j 746 -N 6 memory.dump. Decimal 746 is the address the ROM placed in I. The six bytes there are all 80 in hexadecimal. Each row has only its leftmost bit set, so the same six-byte sprite describes a one-pixel-wide paddle on each side of the screen. The file offset for those bytes is just 0xEA. The extra 0x200 comes from the loader.

Following a call into the score display

A few bytes after the paddles, Pong gives the reader a different exercise. At 0x20E, it loads zero into register VE. At 0x210, the bytes 22 D4 call the subroutine at 0x2D4. To find the subroutine in the ROM, subtract the program base again. File offset 0xD4 is 212 in decimal. From the checkout, od -An -tx1 -j 212 -N 22 roms/Pong.rom shows the complete routine, including its return. Pong program bytes.

02D4  A2 F2   Point I at the three-byte score buffer
02D6  FE 33   Write the decimal digits of VE to that buffer
02D8  F2 65   Load those three bytes into V0, V1, V2
02DA  F1 29   Point I at the font glyph for the digit in V1

Take a hypothetical score of 27. The decimal conversion at 0x2D6 would write three ordinary bytes, 00 02 07, at addresses 0x2F2 through 0x2F4. Loading those bytes puts the tens digit in V1 and the units digit in V2. The font lookup then selects the glyph for 2. With this project's font base and five bytes per glyph, that makes I equal to 0x5A. These are the same font bytes copied during initialization, now used for something a player can recognize. Font, decimal, and register-transfer opcodes.

The rest of the routine supplies the coordinates. It sets V4 to hexadecimal 14, or 20, and V5 to zero. A five-row draw would put the tens digit at (20, 0). Adding hexadecimal 15 to V4 moves the next draw to (41, 0). The routine looks up V2's glyph, draws the units digit, and returns. Its caller would continue at 0x212. With the actual initial VE value of zero, both lookups would select the zero glyph.

This also gives a concrete design question for the unfinished execution loop. My stack helper pushes the current program counter, and the pop helper restores it. To return to 0x212, the call implementation and instruction fetch would have to agree on when to advance by two. If the saved address were still 0x210 when the return completed, the next fetch would call the score routine again. The same two bytes make a perfectly readable listing either way. Only executing the control flow would expose the difference. Stack helpers.

Where the listing ends

The disassembler walks forward two bytes at a time. It will eventually reach those six sprite bytes and try to print instructions for them as well. A reader who follows the pointer in I can recognize the drawing data. The linear scan has no record of how the program uses it. Likewise, seeing a draw mnemonic in the listing tells you what the ROM requests. In this revision, the command-line paths end after disassembly or a memory dump. Rendering those paddles, moving them in response to keys, and advancing the game would require an execution loop and frontend. Command-line entry points.

posts.title: Implementing a Unix Shell in C
posts.excerpt: Two copies of a program are running. What happens when you press Control-Z? A shell lab trace follows the signal from the terminal to the job table.
posts.content:
Start two copies of the same program, leave one in the background, and press Control-Z while the other is running in the foreground. Which copy should stop? How does the shell know when it can print another prompt? These questions are the core of my tiny Unix shell. The CS:APP Shell Lab gave me a driver, helper programs, and traces that make job control observable. My implementation connects the commands at the prompt to the process groups and signals underneath. Shell Lab files.

What the shell remembers

Each entry in the job table holds a process ID, a shell-assigned job number, the original command line, and a state. The process ID is how the shell refers to a child when talking to the kernel. The job number is the short handle you can type as %1 or %2. Keeping the original text lets jobs show that two instances of the same executable came from different commands. At most one entry should be in the foreground. Other entries can be running in the background or stopped. Job states and records.

When I enter ./myspin 4 &, the parser removes the final ampersand from the argument list and reports a background command. For an external command the shell forks, and the child calls setpgid(0, 0) to become the leader of a new process group. It then passes the executable path, arguments, and inherited environment to execve. This explains why the traces spell out paths such as ./myspin and /bin/echo. The implementation passes the first argument directly to the kernel. Launching a command.

Following two jobs through a stop and resume

The ninth trace starts one helper for four seconds in the background and another for five seconds in the foreground. The helper sleeps in one-second increments. After two seconds, the driver sends the shell the stop signal an interactive user would normally produce with Control-Z. It then asks for the job list, resumes job 2 in the background, and asks for the list again. Trace 9.

The foreground lookup is what makes that sequence work. The stop handler finds job 2's process ID and passes its negative to kill. In this call, a negative ID addresses the process group. The background helper belongs to a different group and keeps running. The first listing in the reference transcript shows job 1 running and job 2 stopped. On bg %2, the shell looks up the entry by its job number, sends the group SIGCONT, and records the background state. The second listing shows both jobs running. Their process IDs stay the same throughout. Reference transcript.

When a foreground job has two processes

The two-helper example still leaves room for a subtle mistake. If the stop handler sent a signal to just the individual foreground PID, the first listing would look right. Each copy of myspin consists of a single process. The twelfth trace changes that detail. It launches ./mysplit 4, which forks its own child. The child sleeps in a loop while the original process waits for it. The shell still creates exactly one job-table entry because it directly launched only the original process. Both processes inherit membership in the foreground job's group. Two-process helper.

Trace 12 sends the stop signal two seconds in and then requests both jobs and /bin/ps a. Those commands observe different things. My shell can report its one entry as stopped as soon as the stop handler updates the table. The ps output observes the individual processes. In the saved reference transcript there are two entries for ./mysplit 4, and both have status T, meaning stopped. If the shell had signaled just the leader, the child could have continued sleeping while the job list still looked correct. Group-stop trace. Reference process listing.

Resuming uses the same group identity in the opposite direction. With fg %1, the builtin finds job 1, sets its table state to foreground, sends SIGCONT to the group, and enters waitfg. Both the waiting parent and the sleeping child can resume. The child eventually exits, its parent collects it and exits in turn, and the shell collects the parent. With bg %1, the group likewise resumes, but the shell leaves the prompt available for another command. Looking at which process waits for which child explains why the terminal sees a single job throughout that sequence. Resume and foreground-wait code.

The race between launch and bookkeeping

When a child exits, the kernel can deliver SIGCHLD while the parent is still processing the launch. My handler calls waitpid in a loop, asking for any child whose status is ready. WNOHANG lets the loop finish when there is nothing left to collect. WUNTRACED also reports stopped children. An ordinary exit removes the corresponding job from the table. Collecting child status.

Reading the launch code again, I can see a timing hole. The parent blocks signals before the fork, but unblocks them before adding the new job. A short-lived child can finish in that interval. The handler can collect its exit and find no record to remove. Then the parent inserts a job whose process has already gone. A foreground wait can keep checking that stale entry. Registering the child while the signals are still blocked would give the handler a consistent table when delivery resumes. Signal ordering in the parent.

Signal reporting has a similar gap between intent and observation. The interrupt handler prints a termination message and deletes the job immediately after forwarding SIGINT. Forwarding requests an action from another process. The status returned by waitpid is where the shell can learn how that process actually ended. A program can handle an interrupt itself, for example. The implementation also prints fixed signal numbers in parts of the status handler. Reading the terminating or stopping signal from the returned status would distinguish an interrupt from other reasons a child was stopped or killed. Signal forwarding and status reporting.

The traces capture what a user should see, down to which job stays running. They also explain why the same transcript can look right while an ordering bug survives. A sleeping helper leaves ample time to register the child. A command such as /bin/true can exit while the parent is still returning from fork. The first case tells me where Control-Z went. The second makes me ask whether the shell remembered the job in time to forget it.

posts.title: FP-Growth Algorithm for Market Basket Analysis
posts.excerpt: Six grocery baskets show how a prefix tree compresses transactions, and which counts you need before you can turn a pattern into an association rule.
posts.content:
Suppose three shoppers buy apples and two of them also buy milk. If a fourth shopper arrives with apples, how much reason do I have to expect milk in their basket? My Java market basket project starts several steps upstream of that question. The input has one grocery item per row. Before I can count a combination, I need to decide which rows belong to the same shopping trip.

Deciding what counts as one basket

The parser groups rows by date and member number. Under that definition, milk bought on Monday and apples bought on Friday belong to separate baskets even if the same person paid for both. Two visits from one member on the same date collapse into a single basket. That choice sets a limit on what the result can tell me about individual trips. Transaction grouping in the CSV parser.

I count support by asking how many baskets contain an item. A shopper can buy three cartons of milk and still contribute one observation of milk. The driver sets a minimum support count of 90 for the grocery data. For a small example, I’ll lower it to two and use six baskets where the arithmetic fits on paper. Support counting and item ordering.

1   bread, milk, apples
2   bread, milk, apples
3   bread, milk
4   bread, apples
5   bread
6   milk

Reading a branch of the tree

Bread appears in five baskets, milk in four, and apples in three. I put the most frequent item first in each basket, then insert the items into a prefix tree. The first two baskets follow exactly the same branch. Inserting basket three increments the bread and milk nodes and stops there. Basket four shares the bread node but gives it a second child, apples. Basket six starts a fresh milk branch at the root.

There are now two milk nodes. The one below bread has count three, which means three baskets began with bread followed by milk in the chosen ordering. The one at the root has count one. Adding them recovers the global milk count of four. Reversing that calculation would lose information. A global count of four tells me nothing about which three baskets also had bread. The branching structure carries that evidence. Prefix insertion in FPTree.

What happens when two items tie?

Ordering matters because the tree only shares prefixes that look identical. In the six-basket example, the support counts happen to rank every item unambiguously. Imagine instead two receipts with identical contents, one recorded as bread then milk and the other as milk then bread. Both items have support two. Ideally both receipts increment the same two nodes. That takes a rule for breaking the tie, such as ordering equal-frequency products by name.

There are two sorts in the Java code. The frequency list starts with a map ordered by product name. When sorting each receipt, however, the implementation builds a fresh map in the receipt’s own order and sorts its entries by frequency alone. A stable sort preserves the original order of a tie. Our two receipts can therefore follow different branches. An index of all nodes named milk still lets me recover milk’s total, but the bread–milk pair is split across two different choices of suffix. With a threshold of two, a miner that treats each orientation separately can drop both one-count pieces. I would give every product a position in the global ordering and use that position for every insertion. The two ordering steps.

Following apples back to the root

My tree keeps an index of nodes by item name. Looking up apples finds two nodes. One has count two and the prefix bread, milk. The other has count one and the prefix bread. These weighted paths are the conditional pattern base for apples. Bread gets a total of three and milk gets two. The pair apples and milk therefore has support two. Reading the association in one direction gives a confidence of two out of three for milk given apples. Reading it in the other direction gives two out of four for apples given milk.

Working that example by hand exposes a problem in my final reporting method. Its printed confidence adds the global counts of the suffix item and one prefix item, then divides by the number of retained baskets. For apples and milk that expression gives seven divided by six. A conditional probability above one is enough to show why the report needs the joint count and the antecedent’s count. Both are available for this pair. The rule-reporting code.

Longer combinations need another step. My code pools prefix-item counts and forms subsets with a power set. Two frequent partners of apples might come from entirely separate baskets. To check whether all three occurred together, I need the weighted paths that still preserve those relationships. Han, Pei, and Yin build and mine conditional trees for that purpose. If I continued the project, I’d use the six original baskets to check each reported combination by direct counting before trusting it on a larger file. The original FP-growth paper.

A basket file that separates pairs from triples

Here’s the smallest change I’d make to that hand check to expose the power-set problem. Start a second file with two apples-and-milk baskets, two apples-and-bread baskets, two bread-and-milk baskets, one basket of bread alone, and one of milk alone. Milk and bread each have five observations, apples four. Keep the same support threshold of two. Both apple pairs still qualify. A trip containing all three products has never occurred in this file.

The apple prefix paths retain enough detail to answer the triple question. The milk path has weight two, and the separate bread path also has weight two. Neither path contains both partners. Once those paths are pooled into a map with just the two item names and totals, that distinction disappears. This is a particularly useful case for a data-mining project because every individual count looks plausible even as the resulting combination changes meaning.

I would also keep the original number of baskets alongside the filtered data. Add a seventh receipt to the first file containing only a rare spice. After filtering, it contributes no tree nodes. The apple-and-milk pair still has two occurrences and the confidence for milk given apples is unchanged. Its share of all shopping trips does change, from two in six to two in seven. Remembering that empty receipt matters whenever a report turns an absolute support count into a percentage.

posts.title: Building RESTful APIs with Go
posts.excerpt: Follow a Bitcoin quote from a saved CoinMarketCap response through DynamoDB to a Go HTTP handler. The path explains what a successful lookup can tell you about the quote’s age.
posts.content:
For a software deployment course at SUNY Oswego, I built a service to answer a small question about CoinMarketCap’s top 100 cryptocurrencies. If someone asks for BTC, what name, rank, and dollar price should come back? Making the HTTP route was the shortest part of the job. The interesting decisions were how a quote got there in the first place and what the service could promise about it.

Two programs and one table

The project has two Go programs with different schedules. The collector requests CoinMarketCap’s latest listings, decodes the response, and writes a record for each coin to DynamoDB. The HTTP service accepts requests whenever a reader has a question. It reads the database, so ten people looking up Bitcoin do not trigger ten calls to CoinMarketCap. A reader can also retrieve the last stored price while the collector waits for its next poll. Collector loop.

The upstream response has a nested structure. Each entry carries a name and symbol, a field called cmc_rank, and a quote object containing values for USD. My DBitem type keeps four fields. The collector copies the rank, name, symbol, and price into that type, then sends it to DynamoDB with PutItem. Market capitalization appears in the upstream data, but it drops out at this step. Adding it to the HTTP response later would also require changing what the collector stores.

Following one Bitcoin quote

The repository includes a saved listing with 100 entries. Its Bitcoin record has rank 1 and a USD price of 61422.28861379695. That file gives me a fixed input for tracing a lookup without depending on today’s market. Given that record in the table, a request to GET /mcruz/search?coinName=BTC would produce this JSON, shown here with the whitespace expanded. Saved input record.

[
  {
    "coinRank": 1,
    "coinName": "Bitcoin",
    "coinSymbol": "BTC",
    "coinPrice": 61422.28861379695
  }
]

Even one match comes back in an array because the search handler collects matching records. The parameter is named coinName, yet the server compares it with both the name and the symbol. An empty query gets HTTP 400. A supplied term with no matching record gets HTTP 404. A reader handling both cases can distinguish a missing input from a search that the service actually carried out. Search handler.

The cost of a short request

The URL suggests a direct lookup. Inside the handler, DynamoDB scans the table and returns the four selected fields. The server encodes those records as JSON, immediately decodes them into a Go slice, walks the slice looking for a match, and encodes the matching records again. A small table makes that path easy to follow. It also makes the round trip through JSON easy to overlook. I would have the search handler filter the slice returned by DumpDB and reserve the encoder for the HTTP response.

There is a second limit in the database call. A DynamoDB scan can return one page and a key indicating where to continue. The coursework implementation makes one scan. If the table ever grows beyond that first page, the handler could return 404 for a coin that exists on the next one. A repeatable check would load enough records to force pagination, pick a symbol from the second page, and look it up through the public route. DynamoDB scan pagination.

When the name is almost right

A small input matrix exposes a detail that a successful BTC lookup hides. Given the Bitcoin fixture, Bitcoin, bitcoin, and BITCOIN all match. bItCoIn misses. The handler builds the lowercase and uppercase forms of the stored name and compares each with the query as submitted. That happens to accept the spellings people are likeliest to try. A mixed-case query makes the difference between this implementation and a truly case-insensitive comparison visible.

A second example concerns the shape of the result. Imagine a record with the name and symbol both set to EXAMPLE. Searching for that word would append the record twice. The name and symbol are tested by separate conditions, and each condition appends a match. One route-level check with that invented record would justify a small change to the loop. Test whether either field matches, then append the record once. The sample is deliberately artificial because a successful Bitcoin lookup cannot reveal the duplicate.

These examples also clarify the response format. A script consuming the route needs to check the status before parsing the body. Success gets a JSON array, including the brackets around a single match. The two error branches send text with an HTML content type. Trying to decode that text into a slice produces a parsing error that obscures the more informative HTTP 400 or 404. I would keep those status codes and give every response from the route a documented representation. Name matching and HTTP responses.

How old is the answer?

Consider an upstream response containing a perfectly valid JSON error object and no listings. The collector has a two-second HTTP client timeout, but a server can return an error response well inside that deadline. The fetch path reads the body and proceeds to decode it without branching on the HTTP status. When the data slice is empty, the write loop has no items to refresh. A stored Bitcoin record could still produce a convincing reply afterward. A check on the refresh operation should therefore capture the provider’s status and the number of records accepted as well as the time it took. Upstream request and decoding path.

The collector sleeps for six hours before each fetch, including the first. It then writes one coin at a time. A request arriving midway through a refresh can therefore see records from different polls. The status route reports the table name and item count, and the stored quote has no collection time. A successful BTC lookup establishes that a record exists. To let a reader judge its age, I would store the observation time beside the price and return both. That one field would answer a question no amount of decimal precision can settle.

posts.title: Image Segmentation: Felzenszwalb Algorithm
posts.excerpt: Three pixels are enough to work through a graph-based segmentation by hand and see how two bookkeeping errors in the Java code can move a boundary.
posts.content:
A color picker gives me three numbers for a pixel. Deciding where the object around that pixel ends takes more information. A single step from dark gray to light gray might mark the edge of a painted sign. The same step might occur a hundred times inside a patch of gravel. For my Java coursework I explored how to make that decision with a graph, using the algorithm described by Pedro Felzenszwalb and Daniel Huttenlocher. Efficient Graph-Based Image Segmentation.

Turning the image into edges

The program opens an image through a file chooser and applies a Gaussian blur with ImageJ. Each pixel becomes a vertex. I connect it to the pixel on its right, the one below it, and the two diagonals to its right, wherever those coordinates fall inside the image. When the whole grid has been visited, an interior pixel is connected to all eight surrounding pixels. Generating edges in just four directions visits each neighboring pair once. Neighbor construction.

I sort the edges by increasing weight. Each pixel starts in its own component, so the cheapest edges get the first chance to form regions. A disjoint-set forest stores a parent, rank, and size for each entry. Finding a representative lets me ask whether two far-apart pixels have already become connected through a chain of accepted edges. Joining two representatives updates the region size in one place.

How much graph does a photograph need?

There’s a useful size check hidden in those four directions. For an image three pixels wide and two pixels high, I expect four horizontal edges, three vertical edges, and four diagonals. The graph builder should produce eleven. At a corner, some neighbor coordinates fall outside the grid. With a row only one pixel high, all the vertical and diagonal edges disappear. Those two shapes check the boundary logic without needing to squint at a segmented photograph.

The same arithmetic explains a practical cost. For a grid of width w and height h, the count is (w − 1)h + w(h − 1) + 2(w − 1)(h − 1). A 1920 by 1080 image gives 8,285,402 edge records before the first merge. The Java version keeps these records in a list and sorts the whole list. Each edge also carries endpoint objects and references used to retrieve coordinates and colors. If I were adapting the project to handle larger photographs, I’d start by measuring graph construction and sorting separately from union operations. Replacing the coordinates of an endpoint with its integer pixel index is one way to change the storage cost while preserving the neighborhood and weight calculations. Graph construction and sorting.

Three pixels and one boundary

The decision at the next edge depends on both components it touches. The threshold for a component is its largest accepted edge weight plus k / size. A single pixel starts with internal difference zero. For a concrete first-pass example, take three pixels in a row, two successive edge weights of 4 and 11, and a value of 12 for k.

The edge of weight 4 fits under both singleton thresholds of 12. Joining those two pixels gives a component of size two. Its new threshold is 4 + 12 / 2, or 10. When the edge of weight 11 comes up, the third pixel would accept it, since 11 is below 12. The pair already formed has the stricter limit of 10, so the boundary stays. Changing the second edge to 9 would merge all three. That one calculation shows why the sort order and the component sizes both matter.

How the scale parameter changes a decision

The program starts with k = 1500. The value of 12 above was deliberately small so I could trace a rejection in just three vertices. With the application’s setting, a component of 100 pixels gets an allowance of 15 on top of its largest accepted weight. At 1,000 pixels that allowance shrinks to 1.5. Suppose two such regions both have internal difference 7. An edge of weight 14 clears the smaller region’s threshold of 22, but exceeds the larger region’s threshold of 8.5. Increasing the number of similar pixels behind one side of a boundary can change the decision at its edge.

The Gaussian blur happens before these weights are even calculated. Blurring a sharp transition changes the neighboring colors presented to the graph, while changing k changes the allowance used when combining the resulting components. To understand a result, I would hold the input and blur fixed while varying k, then hold k fixed while varying the blur. The component counts and their areas give me something comparable across runs even when the preview colors change. The starting parameters and processing order.

What the Java version actually computes

Two details in my implementation can change that result. The edge weight was meant to be the Euclidean distance between RGB triples. The source subtracts the starting red channel from the ending green channel, and the starting green from the ending blue. Put two identical pixels with RGB values (10, 40, 90) next to each other. Their intended distance is zero. The current expression gives the square root of 30 squared plus 50 squared, about 58.3. An all-gray example hides the error because its three channel values coincide. The edge-weight calculation.

The second detail concerns which representative survives a merge. On equal ranks, join(a, b) makes b the parent. The segmentation loop writes the new threshold to a and reads the size stored there. In the three-pixel example, the next lookup can therefore reach the surviving root with its old threshold of 12 and accept the edge of weight 11. Looking up the representative after the join would put the new threshold on the component the next edge actually sees. Union and threshold updates.

My application also makes a cleanup pass for components smaller than five pixels, then assigns a random display color to each final representative. To check the three-pixel calculation, I would inspect component membership immediately after the first pass. By the time the preview window opens, cleanup can have joined those tiny regions, and the colors can change each time the program runs. The representatives keep a much clearer record of which boundary the merge rule chose. Cleanup and rendering.

posts.title: My Journey into Computer Architecture
posts.excerpt: A Pentium 4, four integers, and a short x86 loop explain why clock speed tells only part of the story.
posts.content:
The Pentium 4 in the photograph is where my interest in computer architecture began. I’m holding it over a motherboard with the contacts facing the camera. From that side you can see how the package meets the socket. Everything I wanted to understand about the processor happens out of sight. What does it actually do between reading an instruction and making its result available to the next one?

Four numbers and a loop

I like to start with something I can work through on paper. Suppose an array contains four 32-bit integers, 4, 7, 1, and 3. I want their sum. In the following x86 assembly, written in Intel syntax, ESI initially holds the address of the first integer. EAX holds the running total and ECX counts the elements still to visit. Intel’s instruction set reference, volume 2.

xor eax, eax
mov ecx, 4
next_value:
    add eax, [esi]
    add esi, 4
    dec ecx
    jnz next_value

On the first pass the processor reads the integer at the address in ESI and adds 4 to the zero in EAX. Moving the pointer forward four bytes puts it at the second integer. Decrementing the counter leaves three, so the jump takes us back to next_value. The subsequent totals are 11, 12, and 15. On the last pass the decrement produces zero, sets the zero flag, and the conditional jump falls through. Those register values and that final branch outcome are the promises the instruction set makes to the program.

What the processor can do early

The instructions on the page look like a queue of jobs for a single worker. The Pentium 4’s NetBurst design has more options. Its front end decodes x86 instructions into smaller operations. It can keep a sequence of those operations in a trace cache, so a trip around a familiar loop can reuse the decoded work. Farther along, the execution engine can schedule an operation when its inputs and an appropriate execution unit are available. Instructions retire in program order, preserving the state the software expects to see. Intel’s description of the Pentium 4 microarchitecture.

There is a limit you can spot directly in the example. The second update of EAX needs the sum from the first. The pointer update, on the other hand, needs the old address and the constant 4. It can produce the next address without knowing the sum. This is why I draw arrows between inputs and results when I read assembly. Counting six lines of source gives me a poor basis for predicting how long the loop will take. Following the arrows tells me which calculations really have to wait.

Breaking a dependency on paper

There is a simple way to change the example and see what that dependency costs. Keep two running sums. Put 4 and 1 into the first sum and 7 and 3 into the second. The partial results are 5 and 10, and the final addition still produces 15. The order is valid here because the example uses small integers that fit in a register. A floating-point reduction would need a separate discussion about rounding before changing its order.

With two accumulators, an instruction updating the second only needs the previous value of that accumulator. It can overlap arithmetic from the first chain when the inputs and execution resources are ready. Now imagine a longer array with the same layout. A single accumulator has one addition feeding the next for the entire length. The two-way version has two shorter chains and a final addition joining them. It still has to read every element. If waiting for memory dominates that particular run, rearranging the additions may do little for elapsed time.

This thought experiment gives me a way to separate two numbers in a processor manual. Latency answers how long a result takes to become available to an instruction that needs it. Throughput describes how frequently the machine can start or finish operations under suitable conditions. A unit can accept another independent operation while the first one is still in flight. I can exploit that property only if the program supplies independent work. The two running sums make that requirement visible without assigning a cycle count to the particular chip in my hand.

The final trip around the loop

A branch creates a different kind of wait. To keep a deep pipeline busy, the front end predicts where instruction fetching should continue. In this example the backward jump is taken three times and falls through once. If the processor predicts another trip on that last iteration, it can start work that the program will never use. When the branch resolves, younger work from the wrong path is discarded and fetching resumes at the fall-through address. The answer remains 15. The time spent obtaining it depends in part on how well the predictions matched those four outcomes. Intel’s optimization manual, NetBurst branch prediction.

What I would measure

I can change one aspect of the experiment without changing its arithmetic. Put 1,024 integers next to one another, then place the same values 4,096 bytes apart in a second version. The first traversal reads a 4 KiB span. The second visits addresses spread across roughly 4 MiB. A fetched cache line can supply several successive integers in the first layout. The widely spaced layout gives fewer opportunities to reuse the neighboring bytes and also touches more virtual-memory pages.

The placement also matters if I decide to count instructions. The same number of element loads can generate very different amounts of traffic farther down the memory hierarchy. When a block of neighboring bytes has already arrived, another load from that block can be served nearby. A large stride makes a subsequent load more likely to need another block. Repeating a traversal might keep more of one layout resident than the other. Looking only at the static assembly would miss both effects.

Before timing the two, I would make both return the sum, check that the answers agree, and inspect the generated code. Then I’d repeat each traversal with the same data and record whether it was the first or a later pass. That turns an intuition about memory locality into a question a real machine can answer. It is the reason I still like the photograph. A chip small enough to hold in two fingers can run that same handful of instructions in ways the printed program barely hints at.

posts.title: Bringing the M5 MacBook Air’s Internal Display Up on Linux
posts.excerpt: How Linux joined a running display coprocessor, shared its address tables, and kept presenting frames after the panel powered back on.
posts.content:
The 13-inch M5 MacBook Air can already show a picture when Linux starts. Apple's boot firmware has powered the panel, chosen a mode, and left a framebuffer for the next stage. A console can draw into that buffer. The harder milestone was getting Linux to present a new frame through the display coprocessor, receive confirmation that the frame went on screen, and do it again after turning the panel off and on. My patch for the J813 MacBook Air targeted that sequence on the M5's T8142 chip and the H17-generation display firmware supplied with macOS 26. It builds on DjDeveloperr's H17 work. Native M5 Air display patch and hardware report.

Attaching to a display already in motion

The display coprocessor, abbreviated DCP, runs firmware independently of the main CPU. By the time the Linux driver probes it, iBoot has left that firmware running. Its memory mappings are live and some of its translation tables are locked. Restarting the processor would discard the session Linux is supposed to join. I gave the T8142 driver an explicit setting for adopting a live session. It reads the coprocessor's control register and requires the run bit to be set. If that precondition fails, probing ends with an error. Otherwise the driver initializes the RTKit mailbox transport and negotiates with the running firmware. Run-state check. RTKit wake sequence.

The board description says which hardware participates in that conversation. It gives DCP a mailbox with interrupts for send and receive events. It identifies separate DART address translators for the coprocessor and the display subsystem. It also assigns the primary scanout plane to IOMFB surface 2. The loader has aliases for the DCP, display, and display DMA nodes so it can attach the correct memory reservations to each. The DCP and display DART nodes begin disabled in the board file. The loader enables them after preparing the handoff. The presence of the hardware and readiness for Linux to drive it are two different facts in that device tree. J813 display topology.

Agreeing on which memory a device address means

A DART translates an address issued by a device into a physical memory address. The loader has to describe the memory the display firmware already occupies so that Linux keeps it reserved. One firmware segment can span noncontiguous physical pages, and two addresses can refer to the same physical page. The companion m1n1 change walks the inherited translations page by page. Memory already inside a reserved carveout needs its device address recorded. Other pages also need a physical reservation. On the J813 tests, the loader report counted seven regions and fifteen mappings and found that the exported reservations matched the live translations on every boot it checked. Loader change and reservation checks.

There is a second agreement to make inside the kernel. Imagine a firmware page table that maps device pages A and B to physical pages P and Q. Linux prepares a table describing A as P. The tables occupy different memory and Linux's table says nothing about B. Both nevertheless give the same answer for the page Linux needs. The new DART check walks each valid Linux leaf entry and asks whether the firmware entry is valid and points to the same physical page. If every such entry matches, the hardware can keep walking its original table. The extra firmware mapping for B remains available to its owner. Comparing Linux and firmware leaf entries.

Now suppose Linux later requests B as R. A comparison made only at attach time would miss that disagreement. The map path checks each affected page in a firmware-owned slot before accepting a new mapping and returns -EBUSY when the physical addresses differ. It can publish Linux translations into vacant root slots and track which slots Linux installed. It also consults the firmware mappings when asked to translate a shared device address that its own table cannot resolve. Those rules let a live coprocessor and a new kernel refer to the same buffers through the whole session. Checking later mappings and resolving shared addresses.

Giving the firmware a surface to present

After RTKit connects, the display protocol still has to establish a framebuffer surface. H17 asks the host to create its default surface through a callback. The host must make a nested registration call with the surface description, provide room for the firmware's four-byte reply, and then acknowledge the original request. An acknowledgment sent before registration would leave the display engine without a valid surface base. The source documents the resulting DMA fault. The driver also obtains the framebuffer dimensions from the firmware, checks that both fit the supported bounds, and sends the dimensions back before committing the description. The board file therefore needs no table of panel timings copied from another machine. Surface-registration callback. Firmware dimension exchange.

The timing generator presents a different problem. The standard call to program the digital output mode fails on this live H17 panel. The driver source records the firmware error and the consequence. Without a running timing generator, the host receives neither the vertical blank event nor confirmation that a frame swap completed. The H17 path inherits the mode programmed at boot. The panel reports 2560 by 1664 pixels. With the 64-pixel notch region hidden, Linux exposes 2560 by 1600 at 60 Hz. That figure describes the configured display mode. It supplies no measurement of the rate at which a particular application produces new frames. Inherited mode handling. Reported panel geometry and mode.

Why the second power-on needs its own test

Turning the display back on makes the firmware report its modes again. The parser sets a variable-refresh flag when a mode supplies the corresponding information. The old allocator left the mode array uninitialized, so a fixed-refresh mode could inherit a nonzero flag from memory previously used for something else. The result was a plausible-looking mode object that asked the driver to issue the wrong kind of swap. A desktop that had been presenting frames could stall after the display powered back up. The fix allocates a zeroed array. A mode starts with variable refresh off, and the parser turns it on only when it reads the relevant evidence. It applies to the shared parser across chips. Variable-refresh conditions. Mode allocation and parsing.

The hardware results in the pull request are tied to a RAM-booted J813 using public m1n1 and U-Boot with their companion changes. Five fresh boots of the final kernel source reached DCP startup and registered appledrmfb as the console, with no reported DART faults or warnings. A sixth attempt stopped at the preflight before Linux because DCP had not yet settled. Three display power-off and power-on cycles completed with page flips continuing. KDE Plasma 6.6 then provided a Wayland desktop on the internal panel with the built-in keyboard and trackpad. Software rendering produced its frames. The evidence from that series covers internal scanout, power cycling, and interactive desktop use. GPU acceleration, brightness control, a separate cursor plane, external displays, and system suspend remained outside its validation. Test conditions and results from the merged patch.

posts.title: What a Margin Backtest Measures
posts.excerpt: Follow a $40,000 loan through five portfolio observations to see how financing, maintenance usage, and drawdowns diverge.
posts.content:
A portfolio starts at $100,000, falls sharply, and returns to $100,000 by Wednesday. Did the account recover? With borrowed money, the answer depends on which line I’m watching. The holdings can be worth exactly what they were on Thursday while the owner’s equity is still lower. In Testfol Margin Stresser I keep the value of the investments and the debt ledger on separate timelines. That lets me explain the gap down to the dollar.

Start with two balances

The margin simulation accepts a dated series of gross portfolio values, a starting loan, a borrowing-rate configuration, and a maintenance fraction. Once it has a liability for a given date, it calculates equity by subtracting that liability from the value of the holdings. It divides equity by gross value to give the share of the account that belongs to the investor. The debt figure includes interest that has accrued but has yet to post to principal. Margin simulation inputs and output calculations.

For this walkthrough I supplied five invented portfolio values directly to that function. I chose a starting loan of $40,000, a fixed annual borrowing rate of 9%, and a maintenance fraction of 25%. Withdrawals, repayments, tax payments, and margin-funded contributions are all zero. Thursday is a prior-session valuation anchor. Friday is the requested start for interest accrual. With those inputs I can check the portfolio arithmetic independently of historical prices, corporate actions, or where a price provider sets the first observation.

Five observations from the margin simulation, rounded for display
DayHoldingsLiabilityEquityUsage
Thu$100,000$40,000$60,00053.33%
Fri$100,000$40,010$59,99053.35%
Mon$85,000$40,040$44,96062.81%
Tue$53,300$40,050$13,250100.19%
Wed$100,000$40,060$59,94053.41%

Why Monday picks up three days of interest

A $40,000 settled loan at 9% costs $10 for one day under the model’s Actual/360 convention. Friday accrues that first $10. The next price observation is Monday, so the ledger advances through Saturday and Sunday before processing Monday. Its liability increases by $30 between the two closes. There are now $40 of charges since the start. For this particular price path, a loop that charged interest only when a new quote arrived would already be off by $20.

The ledger maintains separate balances for settled principal and accrued charges. Within this example the settled balance stays at $40,000, which makes the $10 figure easy to verify. For a run that crosses a month boundary, the implementation moves earlier months’ accrued interest into principal on the third observed trading day of the new month. It then uses the updated principal for subsequent daily accrual. The posting moves a charge between two ledger balances. The account’s liability already reflected that charge on the day it accrued. Daily accrual and monthly posting.

The fixed rate is convenient for a paper calculation. A variable-rate run can use a dated base rate plus a spread. With tiered rates the code applies each spread only to the principal falling inside that tier, sums the daily charges, and reports the effective annual percentage for the whole balance. As a simple illustration, $100,000 at 6% plus another $50,000 at 5% produces $8,500 in annualized charges, or about 5.67% of $150,000. Applying 5% to the whole balance would understate the model’s daily accrual. Rate and tier calculations.

What 100% usage measures

At a maintenance fraction of 25%, the model reserves one quarter of gross value as required equity. The remaining three quarters form the modeled loan capacity. Margin usage is total liability divided by that capacity. On Monday the calculation is $40,040 divided by $63,750, which gives 62.81%. That number describes how much of a chosen borrowing limit the account has consumed. Looking at the loan as a percentage of the holdings would give a different quantity.

On Tuesday the modeled capacity falls to $39,975, while liability reaches $40,050. The difference is $75, and usage rounds to 100.19%. Equity is still positive at $13,250. It is $75 short of the model’s required equity of $13,325. These two ways of measuring the shortfall give me a quick arithmetic check. The results view records observations with usage at or above 100% as breaches. The five-row calculation continues with the gross values I supplied, including Wednesday’s rebound. A breach marker records what happened to the modeled ratio at an observation. Any forced-sale scenario would also need assumptions about what was sold, at what time and price, and how the proceeds changed the loan. How the chart records breaches.

The maintenance fraction here is an explicit scenario input. The app can also combine per-ticker assumptions using allocation weights. For example, weights of 60% and 40% with requirements of 25% and 50% produce a weighted fraction of 35%. For any particular live account, the broker sets and applies its own requirements. A single allocation-weighted percentage and a closing-price series cannot establish the requirement a broker applied intraday to an individual position. Weighted maintenance in the backtest.

A drawdown needs a named series

The drawdown calculation tracks the highest observed value so far and measures each observation against that peak. For the holdings, Tuesday is $53,300 divided by $100,000 minus one, or −46.70%. Applying exactly the same calculation to equity gives $13,250 divided by $60,000 minus one, or −77.92%. Each dollar of price decline passes through to the owner’s smaller starting equity, and accrued interest adds another $50 to the loss by Tuesday.

Wednesday sets the gross drawdown back to zero. Equity would need another $60 to reach its own earlier peak of $60,000. The episode finder records a recovery date when the series regains its running high. If the final observation is still below that high, a qualifying episode remains open. On these five values it reports Wednesday as the recovery date for holdings and leaves the equity recovery date empty. Both results are correct for the series passed to the function. Drawdown episodes and recovery dates.

Daily-reset leverage changes the path itself

The local engine can also model a ticker with a daily leverage multiplier. To isolate that mechanism, take an underlying that rises from 100 to 110, then returns to 100. Its second return is approximately −9.09%. Isolate a 2× return series by setting its financing contribution and expense drag to zero. The first move takes the series to 120. The second applies roughly −18.18% to that new base, leaving about 98.18. The difference survives even though the underlying made a round trip.

In that calculation the multiplier acts on each session’s return. The earlier $40,000 example instead carried a dollar loan from day to day and charged it calendar-day interest. The code reflects the distinction. The synthetic ticker transforms a return series and can deduct funding and expense terms using a 252-session convention. The account ledger tracks principal, payments, and accrued interest using calendar dates. Putting both on a chart is meaningful when the account actually holds a modeled leveraged instrument and separately borrows cash. For this five-observation example, the gross price path and the account loan are sufficient to reproduce every number in the table. Daily leverage and expense handling.

posts.title: Porting Voice Conversion to MLX on Apple Silicon
posts.excerpt: Follow the hiss and vowel in a single word through pitch estimation, feature retrieval, and synthesis on the Mac.
posts.content:
Say the word “see” and stretch out the vowel. The hiss at the beginning tells a listener which word you said. The vowel carries a pitch you can raise or lower while leaving the word recognizable. A voice converter has to preserve details like that hiss while generating audio with the character of the target voice. When I ported retrieval-based voice conversion to MLX for Apple Silicon, those two sounds gave me a way to reason about what each stage should carry forward.

Starting with a common clock

Consider the Python file-conversion path in the port. The loader reads samples from disk, averages the channels if the file is stereo, and resamples the signal to 16,000 samples per second. The pipeline applies a high-pass filter at 48 Hz and reflects 1,600 samples onto each end. That supplies a tenth of a second of context around both boundaries. A model processing the first vowel now has some audio to its left, just as it would for a vowel in the middle of a sentence. Audio loader and filtering and padding.

A one-second, 48 kHz stereo recording starts with 48,000 sample values per channel. After mixing and resampling, the analysis path has 16,000 mono samples. Padding brings that to 19,200. The pitch path uses a 160-sample hop, so it has a budget of 120 ten-millisecond positions in that padded input. A hop measures the distance between consecutive estimates. It does not restrict the estimator to hearing ten milliseconds of context. That distinction matters when interpreting an abrupt change in pitch at the edge of a syllable.

Two descriptions of the same vowel

The content branch sends the audio through a HuBERT-style encoder. Convolutions produce features a short distance apart, and the encoder refines them using context. Each result is a vector of learned values that helps the synthesizer recover the speech sounds. Keeping the vectors avoids having to transcribe the word, pick a dictionary pronunciation, and reconstruct the original timing from those symbols. It also means that a change to one feature coordinate rarely has a simple name like “more sibilance.” Content encoder.

The other branch estimates fundamental frequency, or F0. On a voiced stretch of “see,” the vibration of the vocal folds produces a roughly repeating pattern. If the pitch extractor reports 110 Hz, the estimated period is about 9.1 milliseconds. On the hiss, a frame may receive zero because there is no stable periodic source to track. That zero is a meaningful input to the converter. The content branch still carries the shape and timing of the consonant. The file runner uses RMVPE as its default pitch method, with other estimators selectable through the same interface. Pitch extractor interface.

Suppose I request a shift of twelve semitones with autotune disabled. The pipeline multiplies each estimate by two raised to the power of the shift divided by twelve. The 110 Hz vowel becomes 220 Hz. Zero stays zero. The code saves those continuous values and makes a second, coarse representation on a mel scale. With the port’s 50-to-1,100 Hz mapping, 110 Hz rounds to bin 23 and 220 Hz rounds to bin 60. An unvoiced frame lands at the lower bin of 1 while its continuous F0 remains zero. Those two arrays now convey different information about precisely the same frame. Transposition and pitch quantization.

Giving the frames the same addresses

The HuBERT front end takes a stride of five followed by six strides of two. Multiply those numbers and adjacent content vectors correspond to input positions 320 samples apart, or 20 milliseconds at 16 kHz. The pitch path advances twice as often. To align the two, the port repeats each content vector. Two consecutive pitch estimates can therefore accompany the same content vector. If the vowel is sliding upward, the pitch estimates can change over those two frames even though the repeated content vector stays identical. Convolution strides.

There is a small edge case hiding in those tidy numbers. The last convolution window must fit its input. Dividing the original sample count by 320 gives the spacing, but it does not establish how many complete feature vectors the convolutions produce. The implementation bounds the length using the smaller of the input’s 160-sample positions and the repeated content sequence, then trims the pitch arrays to that span. When tracking an alignment problem, I would inspect the last frame that goes into the synthesizer before blaming a pitch detector for dropping a syllable. Frame repetition and trimming.

What the retrieval dial changes

If I supply a feature index and select a positive index rate, the converter asks FAISS for eight neighboring vectors for each content frame. It squares the reciprocal of each returned distance and normalizes those weights before combining the neighbors. A neighbor with distance 1 consequently has four times the influence of one with distance 2 before the common normalization. The resulting vector is blended with the original content according to the index rate. This lookup happens before the content vectors are repeated and leaves the pitch estimates alone.

Here is the arithmetic for one imaginary coordinate. Let the original value be 0.20 and the weighted neighborhood value be 0.80. An index rate of 0.75 produces 0.65. With protection set to 0.25, a voiced frame keeps that 0.65. An unvoiced frame blends one quarter of 0.65 with three quarters of the original 0.20, yielding 0.3125. The protection branch is active for settings below 0.5. This gives the hiss more of its input features while letting the sustained vowel use the retrieved ones. The example follows one coordinate for legibility. The actual blend operates over whole vectors. Retrieval weights and unvoiced protection.

Carrying a model across frameworks

The synthesizer combines content and coarse pitch in its encoder, uses an embedding for the speaker ID, and passes a latent representation through the reverse flow. The decoder receives that representation and the continuous F0 contour to generate samples at the model’s output rate. A 40 kHz model needs 4,000 output samples trimmed at either end to remove the tenth of a second of context we added. Trimming 1,600 output samples instead would remove only 40 milliseconds at that rate. Synthesizer inference.

A checkpoint also has an ordering contract. For an ordinary one-dimensional convolution, the conversion tool moves the PyTorch axes for output channel, input channel, and kernel position into MLX’s output channel, kernel position, and input channel order. Transposed convolutions need a different permutation. If two axes happen to have the same length, a mistaken swap can pass a shape check and still connect a coefficient to the wrong channel. A short reference clip and intermediate feature values can locate that error far more precisely than an inspection of the final waveform alone. Checkpoint layout conversion.

For a listening comparison I would keep the same recording and voice model, convert once at zero pitch shift and once at twelve semitones, and listen separately to the onset and the held vowel. For timing I would also specify whether the interval includes file I/O, index retrieval, and writing the output. MLX can defer computation, so a timer around construction of an array expression captures different work from a timer that waits for the samples. One short recording can reveal all three kinds of mistake if I preserve its inputs and ask a specific question at each stage. MLX evaluation semantics.

posts.title: Keeping a Snapdragon Laptop Talking After the Firmware Handoff
posts.excerpt: What a photograph, a framebuffer, and six USB cable pairings can establish about code running on an ASUS Zenbook A16.
posts.imageAlt: q1n1 boot console read back from the Zenbook A16 framebuffer
posts.caption: A later framebuffer readback from the running A16, published in the q1n1 repository.
posts.content:
There are two different ways for a laptop to tell you that it has booted your program. Firmware can print a message on the program’s behalf, or the program can draw one for itself after the firmware has stopped providing that service. Both messages look perfectly convincing in a photograph. For q1n1, the distinction matters. I wanted to know whether code was still running on the Snapdragon after the UEFI handoff, at the Arm exception level the bring-up tools expected. A message printed five instructions too early would answer a much easier question.

q1n1 adapts the bring-up ideas in Asahi Linux’s m1n1 to the ASUS Zenbook A16. The tested machine is the UX3607OA with a Snapdragon X2E-96-100. On an Apple Silicon Mac, m1n1 enters through Apple’s boot environment. The A16 loads q1n1 as a UEFI application. The useful part to carry over is the conversation with a second computer. The part that needs new engineering is everything the laptop must do to stay reachable once firmware stops answering its calls. Project overview and upstream attribution.

Finding the end of the firmware console

Before the handoff, the program can ask UEFI about the current display mode and memory layout. It can also print an error and return. Those conveniences make preflight useful. If the graphics protocol supplies a framebuffer address and usable dimensions, the next stage has somewhere to draw. If the processor reports its current exception level, the program can record where it started. A preflight result still describes an application inside the boot environment. There is another observation to make on the other side.

The handoff itself has a bookkeeping constraint. UEFI gives a caller a memory map and a key identifying that particular map. An allocation between reading the map and handing back its key can make the key stale. q1n1 reserves storage for the map before beginning that exchange. Inside the retry loop it obtains the map, records the descriptor information, and calls ExitBootServices with the returned key. An invalid key can trigger a fresh attempt. The loop avoids unrelated firmware calls such as printing another progress line. At this particular boundary, adding a diagnostic can change the state the diagnostic is supposed to describe. Memory-map capture and handoff.

Drawing a receipt for the handoff

A framebuffer is an area of memory containing the pixels being displayed. Starting a drawing routine requires surprisingly little information, but each piece has a job. The base locates the first pixel. Width and height bound the visible rectangle. The stride says how many pixels of storage separate two successive rows. The pixel format tells the writer which bits represent red, green, and blue. A glyph renderer can draw text using those values without asking firmware to draw a single character.

Consider an illustrative display with eight visible pixels on each row and a stride of ten. Pixel three on row two lives at index 23 when rows and columns start at zero. A calculation using visible width would choose index 19, which is padding at the end of the previous stored row. The first printed row could look entirely correct while the second is displaced and the third begins to wrap strangely. This is why the q1n1 renderer takes width and stride separately. Its initialization also checks the visible geometry against the size advertised for the framebuffer. Framebuffer geometry and pixel writes.

The first hardware record, dated September 16, 2026, reports exception level 2 at entry and again after the handoff. EL2 is the Arm execution level normally used by a hypervisor. The display showed the standalone q1n1 console along with the post-handoff status. A second boot reproduced the observation on the same firmware configuration. Reading the two fields separately matters here. This machine already entered at EL2. Exiting boot services did not itself promote the program to another execution level. First boot and repeat boot records.

From a photograph to a conversation

The photograph preserved a moment. It could show which message reached the screen, but a still image could not tell us whether a heartbeat kept advancing. The early binary also reported that USB serial was unimplemented. Reading a UART description from firmware meant that q1n1 had found some information about a port. It did not mean that a character had passed through a cable to another computer. A useful next milestone was a host receiving a reply generated by code on the A16 after the handoff.

USB brings a second distinction into the experiment. A connector on the enclosure is a physical location. Host and device are roles on a particular connection. The later q1n1 work supported both a serial-class device connection and a network-class connection with the A16 acting as host. A direct cable and a cable routed through a dock can therefore reach the same laptop by different paths. Remembering one serial-device name on the Mac would only find the path that happened to create that name.

In an early experiment a controller enumerated the Mac and the receive path saw 33 Ethernet frames. Three attempted echo requests yielded no reply. Those observations belonged in separate columns of the notebook. Enumeration identified a partner, incoming frames demonstrated one direction of traffic, and there was still no successful round trip. That separation narrowed the next question from “Does USB work?” to “What happens to the return path?” The initial two-port observations.

Moving the cable is part of the test

Independent state for each A16 controller allowed one connection to keep working while the other disappeared. On the Mac, candidate endpoints could be discovered and checked by asking for a valid protocol reply. That design had a physical test that a stationary laptop could never complete. Move the cable to the other port. See whether the old connection is retired, whether the new endpoint is found, and whether the next exchange belongs to the same running stage.

The qualification record describes a revealing failure during a cable move. Device mode could remain marked configured while the controller reported sustained suspend. Waiting exclusively for an explicit disconnect left discovery stuck. Treating every brief suspend as removal would disturb a healthy connection. The recorded fix accommodates short suspends and rechecks a port after an extended one. The native test models both cases. Physically moving the cable supplies the additional evidence that the model represents something this controller actually does. Cable movement and suspend behavior.

Three tested Mac ports and two A16 ports give six direct combinations. Every combination in the record passed a 256 KiB write/read comparison and 100 no-operation requests. The large transfer checks that the bytes returned agree with the bytes sent. The small requests exercise repeated framing. For the dock, one Mac port worked through the dock to both A16 ports, another showed no USB hub on that route, and the remaining pairings were untested. That table is useful precisely because its empty cells survive publication. A reader deciding which topology to repeat can see where the evidence ends. The physical pairing matrix.

What I would keep for the next port

I would keep the early photograph even after getting a much better console. It answers a question about the transition that a later successful USB session can obscure. I would also keep the exact firmware configuration with that photograph, the QEMU run that exercises the binary, and the cable matrix alongside the driver changes. They describe different parts of the system. One shows execution across the handoff on this board, one makes software regressions repeatable, and one records what happens when the physical connection changes.

The payoff for Snapintosh is a machine that can answer questions before a full guest operating system is ready. When an experiment stops producing output, there is a series of smaller observations to revisit. Did firmware start the program? Did the framebuffer show the post-handoff state? Did the selected endpoint return a reply from the current stage? That sequence has proved much more useful to document than a single claim that a laptop boots.

posts.title: What MacGTop’s GPU Percentages Actually Measure
posts.excerpt: Take two samples from one process and work out its share of GPU time. Then follow the numbers into the terminal to see which comparisons hold up.
posts.content:
Imagine a video export slows down. A terminal monitor says the GPU is 61% busy, the window compositor is at the top of a process list, and the tiler and renderer each have a bar of their own. Which number helps explain the export? Before I would blame an application, I’d want to know where each number came from and what interval it describes. Building MacGTop gave me a way to ask those questions of the Apple Silicon GPU from a terminal.

The monitor is written in C. Its display combines information from the I/O Registry with process and power measurements that have different collection paths. Drawing a bar is easy once there is a percentage. The more interesting code decides whether the available data supports calculating that percentage at all. The monitor’s collection and display loop.

Three bars, three driver properties

For the device panel, MacGTop reads a PerformanceStatistics dictionary from the GPU service. The dictionary exposes separate properties for device, tiler, and renderer utilization. The code reads each as an integer and passes the values to the display. That distinction matters when reading a screen capture. The tiler and renderer are parts of a graphics pipeline. Each percentage refers to activity in its own part, and the device figure is a third value supplied by the driver. Adding the two stage percentages together does not produce a meaningful device reading.

Think about two stages working on successive pieces of a frame. Stage B can be working on an earlier piece at the moment stage A starts a later one. A time interval can therefore contain work at both stages. Even if a display shows 50% alongside each, the two labels alone leave the timing of their overlap unknown. The registry code does not reconstruct that timeline. The useful follow-up is to compare how each indicator changes when the workload changes, then look for a GPU trace if the order of the work matters. The three registry readings.

Turning a counter into a rate

The per-process path starts with a different quantity. MacGTop walks the GPU service’s user clients, reads the creator’s process ID, and collects accumulated GPU time from entries in the client’s AppUsage array. A process can own multiple clients, so the code first adds the available counters for the same PID. A single sample now answers “How much time has been counted up to this point?” It takes a second sample and a clock to answer “How quickly is that total growing?” Collecting client counters by PID.

Here is an illustrative pair of samples for a single process with two clients. The counters in this table are in milliseconds for readability. The implementation uses nanoseconds after converting the elapsed Mach clock ticks with the timebase. The second sample is taken 1,200 milliseconds after the first.

Example cumulative GPU time for one PID
SampleClient AClient BSum
First2,000 ms800 ms2,800 ms
Second2,180 ms860 ms3,040 ms

The difference is 240 milliseconds. Dividing 240 by 1,200 and multiplying by 100 gives a process reading of 20%. Dividing by the nominal one-second refresh setting would give 24%. The monitor uses the measured interval because a collection cycle includes work of its own. It walks the registry, collects other fields, formats the output, and then sleeps. A requested sleep duration tells me little about how long all of those operations took together. Elapsed-time calculation and sample retention.

There is another ambiguity in the 20% figure. The process could accumulate those 240 milliseconds in one concentrated burst or in many small bursts spread across the interval. Both histories end at the same counter. For an interactive workload, a burst at the wrong moment can matter more than the average. Shortening the sample interval can show more of the variation, although it also means asking the system for information more often. For an individual missed frame, I would want timestamps for that frame’s work and deadline.

When a row starts at zero

The first time a PID appears, the monitor has no previous counter for it. The calculation also requires the previous accumulated value to be positive and the elapsed interval to be greater than zero. A newly discovered client can consequently appear in the process list before the monitor has a usable rate. The list of candidate processes and the calculation of their rates are separate steps. For example, the discovery code explicitly looks for the window server. To learn whether the compositor dominated that interval, I need to see its counter advance. Finding processes to display.

Changing the set of clients can also change a PID’s total. Suppose a client with a large accumulated time disappears before the next sample. Summing the remaining clients can produce a smaller total even though they continued doing work. The current code subtracts unsigned counters and accepts a delta only if it fits inside the elapsed wall time. A backwards jump typically becomes a very large unsigned difference and fails that check. The next collection stores a new baseline. If I were revising the UI, I’d give an unavailable or discontinuous sample its own mark. Zero recorded activity and a missing pair of comparable readings answer different questions.

Why the history can fool your eye

The device panel includes sparklines, a convenient way to see a busy period after its instantaneous bar has fallen. Looking at the actual display code revealed an important detail of this revision. The loop appends only device utilization to a history buffer. The drawing function receives that one buffer and uses it beside all three bars. The live tiler and renderer values are independent registry readings, but their little historical traces repeat the device series. A screenshot showing three identical peaks does not establish that the stages peaked together. Utilization bars and sparklines.

A useful regression check for a future three-history implementation would feed the renderer deliberately different sequences. Let device utilization rise steadily, tiler activity stay flat, and renderer activity spike in the middle. A person reviewing the output can recognize each pattern immediately. Three synchronized series of realistic-looking numbers would make the wiring harder to verify. This is one of those interfaces where a deliberately simple input can explain a defect better than a beautiful screenshot of a live desktop.

Reading the monitor during an experiment

For a long-running task, I would start with the device reading before the workload begins, keep sampling through the active phase, and let the process rows establish their baselines. Then I would ask whether the proposed explanation fits all three pieces of evidence. Does device activity rise at the expected time? Does accumulated time grow for the process of interest? Does the behavior change in the predictable direction when the workload ends? Those observations can support a hypothesis about who is using the GPU without pretending the monitor measured which shader or command buffer was responsible.

The public revision has one more practical wrinkle. Its JSON output writes the device utilization field, while the interactive screen exposes more of the collected data. Saving that JSON stream is useful for a device-level comparison. It cannot later recreate the process table somebody remembers seeing on screen. I’d decide which question an experiment needs to answer before choosing its recording format. The most useful thing MacGTop gives me is a way to read one number closely enough to know what other measurement to collect next. History, export, and refresh behavior.
